d.title: Three pieces planned, three workers run, three results gathered
d.caption: One planning call, then the three pieces run in **one superstep** rather than one after another — which is the orchestrator's actual advantage over a supervisor, and it is structural rather than a tuning win: **a supervisor cannot parallelise, because it decides who works next only after seeing the last result.** The cost model is `1 + N` calls and the latency is one planning call plus the **slowest** worker.

d.title: The orchestrator's workers must not raise
d.caption: A supervisor's recovery is a **normal turn** — it sees the failure in shared state and retries, switches worker or gives up, for one more coordination call and nothing special. An orchestrator has already fanned out, and the measured run kept the two successes **only because the worker caught its own failure**: **had it raised, the whole superstep would have failed and all three results would be lost** (10.2). So error handling in a worker is structural, not a nicety.

nodes.label: Orchestrator: already fanned out
nodes.sub: no turn left to decide in

nodes.label: The worker caught its own failure
Had it raised: the superstep fails

d.title: A worker cannot see either number, so the decision is not its to make
d.caption: **One failure in three may be fine; three in three is not — and a worker can see neither number, because it does not even know how many siblings it has.** Which is 10.2's fan-out cap argument repeated: the decision needs a view only one node has. So **an orchestrator carries policy in two nodes — the orchestrator bounds the fan-out, the gather node decides what counts as enough — and neither can be pushed down.**

nodes.label: The gather node knows the ratio
Each decision needs a view only it has
nodes.sub: which is why it cannot move

d.title: Six dimensions, and two of them decide it
d.caption: **An orchestrator when the pieces are independent and knowable, because then the parallelism is free and the cost is predictable. A supervisor when the next step depends on the last result, or when you need a decision point between every pair of steps for policy** (12.2). The other four rows follow from those two, and the last row is the one most often forgotten when the parallelism is what attracted you.

columns.title: supervisor
items: a worker failure is a normal turn
policy point: the supervisor, every turn

columns.title: orchestrator
items: a worker failure is the gather node's job

d.title: The worker set stops being topology and becomes runtime state
d.caption: `add_node` runs at build time, so *“add a worker”* normally means editing the graph and redeploying. One generic executor reading a dict of specs removes that — **and moves the worker set out of the code and into data, which is the entire point and also the entire cost.** Notice what the executor already does with an unknown or disabled name: it **degrades** and records why, rather than raising.

nodes.label: One generic executor
nodes.sub: it reads a spec and runs it

nodes.label: The worker set is now runtime state

d.title: One node in the drawing, whatever the registry contains
d.caption: **This is worse than 8.8's `Command` problem: that hid the destinations inside node bodies, and an annotation could recover them for the renderer. Here the worker set is not in the code at all, so there is nothing to annotate** — the set is a runtime value. Which forces a deliberate replacement: **the registry has to become the documentation**, through a listing endpoint or by living in version control. Otherwise the only way to know what the system can do is to read a database.

nodes.label: Here there is nothing to annotate
nodes.sub: the set is a runtime value

nodes.label: So: a listing endpoint
nodes.sub: or the registry in version control

nodes.label: Or else: read a database to find out

d.title: One run must see one worker set
d.caption: **A run that started before a worker was disabled may route to it afterwards, so the registry read has to be atomic per run — a snapshot carried in state or context (10.7), or a pinned registry version.** Read per node execution, a single run can see two worker sets, so **the trace records decisions made against configurations that never coexisted, and no amount of logging recovers which was in force when** — 10.9's version-pinning argument exactly.
vars: worker sets one run can see

steps.note: one bad worker is not an outage

d.title: A canary is a row, and a row is not a measurement
d.caption: Genuinely easier than the compiled version, **where two variants of a worker means two nodes and a conditional edge weighted by a random number.** The caution is that **a canary needs per-variant measurement to mean anything, so the trace has to record which variant ran** — the same point as 10.5's *record which exit fired*. A 5% canary whose results are pooled with the other 95% has shipped a variant and measured nothing.

nodes.label: A variant is a row with traffic: 0.05
Compiled: two nodes and a weighted edge
But a row is not a measurement
So the trace records which variant ran

d.title: The test is whether the workers differ in configuration or in structure
d.caption: **Workers differing only in configuration — a prompt, a tool list — are rows one executor serves. Workers differing structurally make the executor grow a branch per worker, at which point you have reinvented the graph badly.** The frequency test is the other half: **if the worker set changes a few times a year, a deploy is cheaper than a registry, a listing endpoint and a version-pinning scheme** — all three of which this lesson showed you need.

nodes.label: Added often, by people without deploys
nodes.sub: the case it is built for

nodes.label: You have reinvented the graph badly
Changes a few times a year?

d.title: B received the human's message and A's output, with nobody designing a payload
d.caption: Both halves of the trade are real. **The benefit is context for free — B knows what was asked and what A found, and no interface had to be written** — which is why shared state is the right default inside one graph. **The cost is that A's working notes are in B's prompt and B pays for them**, and 12.2 noted it compounds across a supervisor loop, since every worker's output reaches every later worker.

d.title: The worker saw one key, and not the one that mattered
d.caption: `keys=['piece']` — **`secret` was in the parent state and did not cross.** So `Send` is the mechanism for agent-to-agent isolation **inside one graph**, and the right default when one agent's context should not reach another, **which is 12.1's second structural reason for splitting agents at all**: the isolation is the reason for the split, so it would be odd to split and then share everything anyway.

d.title: One field, and two separate things depend on it
d.caption: **An agent cannot weigh information it cannot attribute: a claim from the retrieval agent and a guess from the summarising agent should not carry equal authority, and without `name` they are both just assistant turns.** The second reason is 12.8's: when the output is wrong, *“which agent said that”* has to be answerable from the history. **Nothing in the runtime sets `name`**, so it is a deliberate choice every agent has to make.

d.title: 10.9's three concerns, and then one design question
d.caption: Across a service boundary the payload must be JSON-able — **a LangChain message object is; a graph's full state with reducers is not** — there is a hop per handoff, and the peer can crash, which 10.9 measured as **an empty line rather than an error.** Then the real question: **the whole conversation is simple and grows without bound and crosses the wire every hop; a task-specific payload is bounded and leaves the receiver without context it might need.**

nodes.label: A crash returns an empty line

d.title: Three choices inside a graph, two across services, and one that is not optional
d.caption: The last row is the one that applies either way: **record the handoff itself — who handed to whom and why.** That is the trace 12.8's blame problem needs, and the reason 8.8 argued for `Command` carrying the reason **with** the destination rather than leaving it to be reconstructed from state afterwards. Across services, the conversation **id** is what lets a bounded payload stay bounded without blinding the receiver.

items.label: Shared state for the conversation
items.sub: context for free, inside one graph

items.label: Send for anything a worker should not see
An explicit task payload with a schema
Plus the conversation id
items.sub: so the receiver can fetch history

d.title: Neither is wrong; the failure is choosing one without noticing
d.caption: **“I was charged twice” became “check duplicate charge” — a reasonable summary that loses the user's own words**, which may matter for tone, for quoting back to them, or for a detail the summariser judged irrelevant. Shared state keeps everything and pays for it; a payload is bounded and drops whatever the first agent did not think to include. **Guard: pass the conversation id with the payload, so the receiver can fetch rather than hope.**

d.title: Check-then-act cannot work when the check and the act are the same step
d.caption: The work-done key worked here — **searches performed: 1**, because the writer checked before acting. It only works **with shared state**: with a task payload each agent is blind to the others' work unless the payload says so. **And in a parallel fan-out it does not work at all, because 8.6's superstep means both workers read the same snapshot, so neither sees the other's claim.** So deduplication in a fan-out belongs in the **orchestrator, before the fan-out**.

nodes.label: A work-done key in shared state
In a fan-out: the same snapshot
So neither worker sees the other's claim
nodes.sub: check and act in one step

d.title: No single agent is wrong, and there is no message to point at
d.caption: Attribution via `name` is only half of it. **The harder version: B's output was reasonable given what A passed it, and A's output was reasonable given the question — so no agent is wrong and the system is.** The only thing that helps is **recording the handoffs with their reasons, so the chain of “why did you give it that” is reconstructable** — 8.8's argument for `Command` carrying the reason, and 5.7's auditability principle once more.

nodes.label: A was reasonable, given the question
B was reasonable, given A's handoff
So the system is wrong and nobody is
Then 'why did you give it that' is answerable

d.title: Six failures, and the right-hand column is the content
d.caption: **Two of the six can only live in shared state**, because no agent and no payload can see what they need — the hop count and what has already been done are both properties of the system. **One lives on every message** (`name`), one in the handoff payload (the conversation id), and two are 11.8's guards arriving unchanged. Note there is no row whose answer is *“write a better prompt”*.
